svg.title: Sizing a load test with Little's law
svg.desc: Little's law says L equals lambda times W: L is how many are inside the system (virtual users, or requests in flight), lambda is the arrival rate in requests or sessions per second, and W is the time each one stays (response time, plus think time for a user). Left, the closed model, asking how many virtual users are needed: lambda is the 120 requests per second target, W is 0.15 seconds of response time plus 4.85 seconds of think time, which is 5.0 seconds, so L is 120 times 5.0, which is 600 virtual users. If responses slow to 1.15 seconds, W becomes 6.0 seconds and the same 600 virtual users send only 600 divided by 6.0, which is 100 requests per second, so the test eases off by 17 percent exactly when it matters. Right, the open model, asking how many requests are in flight: lambda is fixed at 120 requests per second by the executor and W is the response time of a single request, so at 0.15 seconds L is 120 times 0.15, which is 18 in flight; at 1.15 seconds the load stays at 120 per second and L is 120 times 1.15, which is 138 in flight, so pre-allocate at least 138 virtual users plus headroom.

g.text: Little's law sizes a load test: L = λ × W
response time (+ think time for a user)
W = 0.15 s response + 4.85 s think = 5.0 s
the test eases off by 17% when it matters
Open model: how many in flight?
λ = 120 requests/s, fixed by the executor
W = response time (one request per iteration)
At 1.15 s the load stays at 120/s, so:
pre-allocate at least 138 VUs, plus headroom
Size VUs from rate × time per iteration, then check the slowest latency you want to test.
